title: Ag an dhochtúir / At the doctor
bridge: In Irish, unlike English, the verb 'to be' is used to describe temporary states like feeling unwell, e.g., 'Tá mé tinn' (I am sick). Additionally, Irish often uses the prepositional pronoun 'agam' (at me) to indicate possession of an ailment, which can be confusing for English speakers. Be cautious with word order, as Irish typically places the verb before the subject in questions.
rule: To talk about health issues in Irish, use the verb 'bí' (to be) for temporary conditions and the prepositional pronoun 'agam' to indicate where the pain or issue is located. For example, 'Tá an tinneas cinn agam' (I have a headache). Questions are formed by placing the verb before the subject, e.g., 'An bhfuil dochtúir agat?' (Do you have a doctor?).

title: Céad mile fáilte! / A Hundred Thousand Welcomes!
bridge: In Irish, booking accommodation involves specific phrases and structures that differ from English. For instance, Irish uses the verb 'taobh' (to book) with the preposition 'le' (with), which might feel unfamiliar. Additionally, Irish often omits the subject pronoun, unlike English where 'I' or 'you' are commonly used. Be cautious of word order and the use of the initial mutation (séimhiú) after certain prepositions.
rule: To book accommodation in Irish, use the phrase 'Ba mhaith liom... a chur in áirithe' (I would like to book...). The verb 'chur' (to put) is used in this context. After 'le', the initial consonant of the following word is lenited (e.g., 'le + teach' becomes 'le theach'). Remember to use the correct prepositions and pay attention to initial mutations.

title: An tSeirbhís Airgeadais / Banking Services
bridge: In Irish, banking terms often use more literal translations compared to English. For example, 'banc' is straightforward, but 'ata' (account) is less intuitive for English speakers. Be cautious with false friends like 'cuntas' (account), which sounds similar to the English word but has a different spelling and pronunciation. Additionally, Irish word order can differ, especially with prepositional phrases, so pay attention to sentence structure.
rule: When discussing banking or currency exchange in Irish, use the verb 'tá' (is) for present tense statements and 'ba' for past tense. Prepositions like 'ar' (on) and 'ag' (at) are crucial for location. For example, 'Tá an t-airgead agam' means 'I have the money.' Currency names are often borrowed from English but may have slight pronunciation differences, e.g., 'euro' is pronounced /ˈɛʊrə/ in Irish. Always use the correct article: 'an' for singular feminine nouns and 'an' for singular masculine nouns starting with a vowel.

title: Ag déanamh iarratais ar phost / Job Interview Basics
bridge: In Irish, unlike English, verb conjugations change significantly based on the subject. For example, 'I work' is 'Oibrím' while 'you work' is 'Oibríonn tú'. Additionally, Irish often uses the verb 'bí' (to be) + the verbal noun for ongoing actions, similar to 'I am working' being 'Táim ag obair'. Be cautious with word order, as Irish typically follows a VSO (Verb-Subject-Object) structure, which is different from English's SVO.
rule: When discussing job interviews in Irish, use the present tense for general statements and the future tense for plans. The future tense is formed by adding 'beidh' (will be) + the verbal noun. For example, 'Beidh mé ag obair' means 'I will be working'. Always use the correct pronoun and verb agreement, and remember that Irish often omits the subject pronoun when it’s clear from context.

title: Ag an bPost / At the Post Office
bridge: In Irish, unlike English, the preposition 'ag' is used to indicate location at a place like the post office, which contrasts with English's use of 'at'. Additionally, Irish verbs often conjugate differently based on the subject, so phrases like 'I am sending' become 'Táim ag seoladh', with 'ag' linking the verb to the action. Be cautious of word order, as Irish typically places the verb before the subject in questions, e.g., 'An bhfuil post agat?' instead of 'Do you have mail?'.
rule: To talk about being at the post office or performing actions there, use the preposition 'ag' followed by the verbal noun. For example, 'Táim ag seoladh litreach' means 'I am sending a letter'. Questions are formed by placing the verb first, e.g., 'An bhfuil stamp agat?' for 'Do you have a stamp?'. Remember that 'ag' is also used for possession in some cases, e.g., 'Tá post agam' means 'I have mail'.

title: Conas Apairtment a Aimsiú / How to Find an Apartment
bridge: In Irish, when discussing renting a flat, the verb 'to rent' is 'cíosú', which is regular and differs from English 'rent'. Be cautious with false friends like 'apartment', which is 'apairtment' in Irish, pronounced similarly but with a distinct stress. Irish also uses the preposition 'ar' for 'on' or 'at' when discussing availability, unlike English 'on' or 'available'.
rule: To talk about renting, use the verb 'cíosú' (to rent) in the present tense: 'cíosaim' (I rent), 'cíosann' (he/she rents). For availability, use 'ar fáil' (available) with the preposition 'ar' (on/at). Questions often start with 'An' (Do/Does) followed by the verb: 'An bhfuil apairtment ar fáil?' (Is there an apartment available?).

title: Ag caint le daoine nua / Talking to new people
bridge: In Irish, when meeting someone new at a party, you often use more formal language initially, unlike in English where informal language is common. Irish also has specific phrases for expressing interest in someone’s background, which can sound overly formal to English speakers. Be cautious with pronouns and verb forms, as Irish uses different structures for 'you' (singular and plural) compared to English.
rule: When introducing yourself or asking about someone’s background in Irish, use the phrase 'Conas a dtugtar ort?' (What’s your name?) and 'Ceist ar do chuid Gaeilge?' (Do you speak Irish?). For expressing interest, use 'Tá suim mhór agam i...' (I’m very interested in...). Remember, Irish uses the verb 'tá' (is) for the present tense, and adjectives follow nouns. Avoid direct translations from English, as word order and grammar differ significantly.

title: Comhhrá: Gearán agus Leithscéal / Conversation: Complaining and Apologizing
bridge: In Irish, complaining and apologizing often involve more formal and indirect expressions compared to English. For instance, Irish speakers tend to use conditional phrases like 'Ba mhaith liom...' (I would like...) to soften complaints, whereas English speakers might be more direct. Additionally, Irish apologies often include phrases that express regret or acknowledge the inconvenience caused, which can sound more elaborate than the straightforward 'Sorry' in English.
rule: To complain in Irish, use phrases like 'Tá mé ag gearán go...' (I am complaining that...) or 'Níl mé sásta...' (I am not satisfied...). For apologies, common expressions include 'Tá brón orm...' (I am sorry...) or 'Leithscéal a dhéanamh duit...' (Excuse me...). Note that the verb 'tá' (is) is often used to express states, and the prepositional pronoun 'duit' (to you) is essential for addressing the recipient directly. Be mindful of the initial mutations (e.g., 'leithscéal a dhéanamh duit' becomes 'leithscéal a dhéanamh leat' when addressing 'you').

title: Mo Bhaile / My Hometown
bridge: In Irish, describing your hometown often involves using the prepositional pronoun 'i' to indicate location, which is different from English's use of 'in'. Additionally, Irish uses the verb 'tá' (is) for present tense descriptions, which is simpler than English's verb conjugations. Be careful not to directly translate 'my hometown' as 'mo bhaile' is the correct phrase, and remember that Irish word order can be more flexible than English.
rule: To describe your hometown in Irish, use the structure 'Tá [location] i [place]'. For example, 'Tá mo bhaile i gContae Chill Chainnigh' (My hometown is in County Kilkenny). The prepositional pronoun 'i' is used to indicate location, and 'tá' is the present tense of 'to be'. Adjectives follow the noun they describe, unlike in English. For example, 'Tá sé beag' (It is small).

concept_examples.text: Tá mo bhaile i gContae Chill Chainnigh.
concept_examples.translation: My hometown is in County Kilkenny.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'hometown' as 'hometown' in Irish, but the correct term is 'mo bhaile'. Remember to use Irish vocabulary and avoid direct translations from English.

Use 'ann' to indicate location, similar to 'there' in English.

Use 'is maith liom' to express liking, similar to 'I like' in English.

examples.note: Conditional phrases like 'ba mhaith liom' are used for wishes.

title: Mo Ghsta / My Hobbies
bridge: In Irish, unlike English, the verb 'to like' (gusta) is often replaced by the prepositional construction 'tá suim agam i' (I have an interest in) when talking about hobbies. Additionally, Irish uses the preposition 'le' (with) to indicate the activity, which might feel unnatural to English speakers. Be cautious not to directly translate 'I like' as 'Is maith liom' is used for preferences, not hobbies.
rule: To talk about hobbies in Irish, use the structure 'Tá suim agam i + activity (le)'. For example, 'Tá suim agam i ríomhclárú le cluichí' (I have an interest in programming with games). The preposition 'le' is used to introduce the activity. Note that 'le' lenites the following word if possible. For sports, you can also use 'imigh chun' (to go to) as in 'Imigh chun hurlaíochta' (to go to hurling).
